title: CRUSH: Contextually Regularized and User anchored Self-supervised Hate speech Detection
measurement_description: The paper primarily evaluates the performance of different contextualized language models (including their proposed CRUSH model) on hate speech detection and scoring tasks. In relation to religion, the paper measures the negative stereotypes and biases absorbed by their hate-infused language model (HateLM) by analyzing its top-3 next-word predictions when prompted with specific religious identity terms (e.g., 'muslim', 'jews').
findings: The study found that continually pre-training a language model on a hateful corpus (creating HateLM) to improve hate speech classification also infuses the model with severe stereotypes against religious groups. When prompted with the word 'muslim', HateLM predicted 'terrorist', 'evil', and 'shit', and for 'jews' it predicted 'idiots', 'bad', and 'stupid'. The authors highlight this as an ethical concern, noting that models can become biased against protected groups depending on the dialect and training data distribution.
